name: Erebos
lines: Erebos, the Underworld of Hades

Crossing the Acheron with Charon
Past Cerberus with the Sibyl's honey cake
Charming Cerberus with Orpheus's tune
The twelfth labour: Cerberus bare-handed
Judged worthy of Elysium
Leading Eurydice up to the light
The trial of Orestes: the Furies made kindly
Rolling Sisyphus's boulder
Beating the Hydra of Tartarus
The Elysian footrace
The Elysian discus
Choosing a life at the Spindle of Necessity
Hermes's tour of the Underworld
A lesson in the Hall of Shades
The Psychopomp's examination
Leaving by the Gate of Horn
Charon's obol (a silver coin, given back)
A crumb of the Sibyl's honey cake
A gut string from Orpheus's lyre
A link of Cerberus's chain
Minos's verdict on a clay tablet
A gold tablet of the initiates
A white flower Eurydice gave you
A torch of the Kindly Ones
A pebble from Sisyphus's hill
A fang of the Hydra of Tartarus
An Elysian laurel crown
A lot drawn from the lap of Lachesis
A feather from Hermes's winged cap
A wax tablet of notes
The Psychopomp's staff
A sliver of the Gate of Horn
a Fury of Tartarus
A scale from a Fury's serpent hair
The Empusa's bronze sandal
an ember hound of the Phlegethon
An ember hound's fang
a fire shade of the Phlegethon
A coal of the Phlegethon that never cools
A Harpy's iron feather
a giant of the old war
A giant's bronze ring
the Hydra of Tartarus

Here at the southern tip of Greece, the ancients said, a cave goes down to the house of Hades. Heracles came this way to fetch Cerberus, and Orpheus to fetch Eurydice. I am Hermes, guide of souls: the dead come down with me, and so, today, do you.
The Vestibule and the Elm of False Dreams

Virgil's Aeneas saw this: a great elm spreading its old arms, and under every leaf a false dream clinging. Round the doorway stand Grief and Cares, pale Disease, sad Old Age, Fear, Hunger, Want, Toil, Death and Death's brother Sleep, and the iron chambers of the Furies.

Centaurs, two-shaped Scylla, hundred-handed Briareus, the Hydra of Lerna, the Chimaera breathing fire, Gorgons, Harpies, three-bodied Geryon. Aeneas drew his sword on them, and the Sibyl stopped him: they are empty shapes, shadows without bodies. Try it yourself.
The Acheron and Charon

The river of woe, and Charon the ferryman in his patched sail and filthy cloak, his eyes like flames. The Greeks put an obol, a small silver coin, with their dead to pay him. Those who were never buried must wait on this shore a hundred years.
The Gate and Cerberus

Hesiod says Cerberus fawns on everyone who comes in, wagging his tail and ears, but lets no one out again. Three heads in most of the stories, a mane of snakes and a serpent for a tail. Heracles carried him up to the light as his twelfth and last labour.
Myrtle woods for those who died of love. Here Aeneas met Dido, Queen of Carthage, and wept; she would not speak to him, and turned back into the shadows.
The Crossroads and the Judges

Plato tells it: three judges sit at the place where the road divides. Minos holds the golden sceptre and gives the final word; Rhadamanthus judges those from Asia, Aeacus those from Europe. The good go right, to the Isles of the Blessed; the wicked left, down to Tartarus.

Homer's meadow of asphodel, where the shades of the ordinary dead drift and murmur. Odysseus met Achilles here, who told him he would rather be a poor man's hired hand on earth than king of all the dead.

The house of Hades and Persephone, which the poets call broad-gated, with its bronze threshold. Hades is lord of the dead and of the riches under the earth; Persephone is his queen for half the year, for she ate the seeds of a pomegranate here.

The gold tablets buried with the initiates told them: on the left of the house of Hades is a spring with a white cypress by it; do not go near. Further on is cold water flowing from the Lake of Memory, with guardians before it. Tell them who you are.

Virgil saw a fortress under a cliff, ringed by three walls and by the Phlegethon's racing flames, its gate held by columns of adamant, an iron tower, and Tisiphone, a Fury, sitting there night and day. Below lies Tartarus, as far beneath as the sky is above.
The Cave of Sleep and the Gates of Dreams

Ovid's Cave of Sleep, where no cock crows and the Lethe murmurs over pebbles, and the sons of Sleep, Morpheus, Phobetor and Phantasos, shape the dreams of the world. Beyond are the two gates of dreams: true ones through the gate of horn, false ones through the ivory gate.
A stranger knocks at your door at night, lost and hungry. The Greeks held xenia, the law of guests, sacred to Zeus. What do you do?
Take them in, feed them, and ask their name only after
Send them on to the next house
Charge them for the bed
Who carries the souls of the dead down to Hades?
Hermes, the guide of souls
You find a body by the roadside, unburied. What did the Greeks believe you owed it?
Three handfuls of earth at least, so the soul can cross
What did the dead need to pay Charon?
An obol, a small silver coin
Which of these was punished in Tartarus for trying to cheat death itself, twice?
Fairness: settle it justly, not by force
Take what you want
Shame him in the market
The quiet life of a private person, minding their own affairs
Odysseus, drawing last, chose this: he had had enough of ambition. He found it lying in a corner where everyone else had passed it by, and said he would have chosen it first.
The life of a swan
Orpheus chose to be a swan, Er saw, rather than be born of a woman again.
The life of a nightingale
Thamyras the singer chose the nightingale's life.
The life of a lion
Ajax, son of Telamon, chose the lion's life: he still remembered the judgement of the arms.
The life of an eagle
Agamemnon chose to be an eagle, from hatred of mankind for all he had suffered.
The life of an athlete
Atalanta chose an athlete's life, seeing the great honours it held.
The life of a skilled craftswoman
Epeius, who built the wooden horse, chose to be a woman skilled in crafts.
The life of a tyrant
The first to choose took the greatest tyranny, and only afterwards saw it held the fate of eating his own children. He wept, and blamed everyone but himself.
Styx, the hateful: the gods swore their great oaths by her water, and a god who broke one lay breathless for a year (Hesiod).
Acheron, the river of woe, where Charon keeps his ferry.
Lethe, forgetting: the dead drink and forget their lives.
Phlegethon (or Pyriphlegethon), the river of fire, round Tartarus.
Cocytus, the river of wailing, a branch of the Styx.
Which river did the gods swear by?
An obol was a small silver coin of ancient Greece: six made a drachma.
The Greeks placed one with the dead, often in the mouth, to pay the ferryman.
Archaeologists have found such coins in graves all over the Greek world.
The unburied could not cross: they wandered the shore for a hundred years (Virgil).
Where was the obol often placed?
In the mouth of the dead
Minos, Rhadamanthus and Aeacus were sons of Zeus, famed for justice in life.
In Plato's Gorgias, Rhadamanthus judges souls from Asia, Aeacus those from Europe, and Minos has the final word.
Homer shows Minos holding a golden sceptre, giving judgement among the dead.
Aeacus later was said to hold the keys of Hades.
Who gave the final judgement?
Hesiod: a bronze anvil falling from the sky would fall nine days and nights to reach the earth, and nine more to reach Tartarus.
It is walled with bronze, and Night is poured round it in three rows, like a collar round a neck.
The Titans were shut in it after their war with the Olympians; the Hundred-Handed guard them.
Later poets put the great wrongdoers there: Sisyphus, Tantalus, Ixion, the Danaids, Tityos.
How long would an anvil fall from earth to Tartarus?
Nine days and nights
Elysium and the Isles of the Blessed
Homer: the Elysian plain at the ends of the earth, where life is easiest, with no snow or storm, only the west wind.
Pindar: the Isles of the Blessed, where breezes blow from the ocean and golden flowers blaze, by the tower of Kronos.
Virgil: Elysium has its own sun and its own stars, and heroes there wrestle, dance and sing.
Only the very good, the heroes, and those judged three times pure went there.
What did Virgil say Elysium has of its own?
Its own sun and stars
Persephone and the seasons
The Homeric Hymn to Demeter: Persephone was picking flowers, and reached for a wonderful narcissus, when the earth opened and Hades carried her off.
Her mother Demeter searched the world with torches and, in her grief, let nothing grow.
Zeus sent Hermes to bring her back, but she had eaten a pomegranate seed below.
So she stays part of every year with Hades: then it is winter; when she comes up, spring comes with her.
What did Persephone eat below?
Orpheus and Eurydice
Eurydice died of a snake bite on her wedding day (Ovid, Virgil).
Orpheus went down through Taenarum and sang to Hades and Persephone, and even the Furies wept; Sisyphus sat on his stone.
They let her follow him up, on one condition: he must not look back until they were out.
At the very edge of the light he turned, and she slipped back into the dark, saying a last farewell he could barely hear.
What was the one condition?
Heracles and Cerberus
The twelfth labour of Heracles was to bring Cerberus up from Hades (Apollodorus).
Hades allowed it if he could master the dog without weapons.
Heracles gripped him round the neck and would not let go, though the serpent tail bit him.
He showed Cerberus to King Eurystheus, who hid in a jar, and then took the dog back down.
What did Hades forbid Heracles to use?
The Furies and the first court
The Erinyes (Furies) punished crimes against family, above all murder: Alecto (unceasing), Megaera (grudging), Tisiphone (avenger of murder).
Aeschylus's Eumenides (458 BC): they hunt Orestes, who killed his mother to avenge his father.
Athena set up a court of citizens on the Areopagus hill to judge him: the first trial by jury in the stories.
The votes were equal; Athena's vote freed Orestes, and she gave the Furies a home and honour in Athens, as the Kindly Ones.
Where did Athena hold the trial?
The Areopagus in Athens
Plato, Republic book X: Er, a soldier killed in battle, woke on his funeral pyre after twelve days and told what he had seen.
Souls came to a meadow, then to the Spindle of Necessity, where the three Fates sing: Lachesis the past, Clotho the present, Atropos the future.
Each soul drew a lot and chose its next life: 'the blame is the chooser's; God is blameless'.
Then they drank from the river of Unmindfulness on the plain of Lethe; the wise drank only a little.
Who chose the quiet life of a private person?
Thin gold leaves inscribed with directions for the dead have been found in graves in Greece and southern Italy, from the 400s BC on.
They warn: do not drink from the spring by the white cypress (forgetting); go on to the Lake of Memory.
The dead must say to its guardians: 'I am a child of Earth and starry Heaven'.
They were buried with initiates of mystery cults that promised a better life after death.
What tree stands by the spring of forgetting?
Odyssey book 11: Odysseus calls up the dead at the edge of the world and speaks with Tiresias, his mother, and Achilles.
Aeneid book 6: Aeneas goes down with the Sibyl of Cumae, carrying the golden bough as a gift for Proserpina, and sees the whole underworld.
Aristophanes' Frogs (405 BC): the god Dionysus rows across the lake with Charon while frogs sing 'Brekekekex koax koax'.
Aeneas leaves by the ivory gate, the gate of false dreams: scholars still argue why.
What did Aeneas carry as a gift for Proserpina?
Grief and avenging Cares have made their beds in the very jaws of the underworld.
Avenging Cares (Virgil, Aeneid 6.274).
Pale Diseases live here.
And Hunger, that counsels wrong.
And shameful Want: shapes terrible to see.
Then Death, and Death's own brother, Sleep.
Sleep, the brother of Death (Hesiod calls them both children of Night).

Virgil, Aeneid book 6: Aeneas and the Sibyl passed them on the way down, 'through the empty halls of Dis and his insubstantial kingdom, like a path through woods by the grudging light of a fitful moon'.
The cave back up to the light
climb up to Cape Taenarum
"Easy is the way down to the underworld: the door of black Dis stands open night and day. But to retrace your steps and come out to the upper air, that is the task, that is the labour."
The Sibyl of Cumae says this to Aeneas before they go down. Every step of this stair is a step down; every step back up is a step against the dark.
Your teeth are made of sugar and it is raining.
You can fly, but only a hand's breadth off the ground, and only on Tuesdays.
Every door in your house opens onto the same corridor.
You have won a race you do not remember entering.
Someone you have never met is waiting for you with a key.
look up into its leaves
"In the midst an elm, shadowy and huge, spreads its boughs and aged arms: the seat, they say, where false Dreams cling, under every leaf."
One drifts down and settles on your shoulder. For a moment you dream it:
It is a false one. They always are, here: true dreams come out of the gate of horn, far in the north-east.
"...and mad Discord, her snaky hair bound up with bloody ribbons." (Aeneid 6.280)
Strife (Eris, to the Greeks) threw the golden apple that began the Trojan War.
Briareus, the hundred-handed
the Hydra of Lerna
The shapes of monsters
